[SPEAKER_04]
Ladies and gentlemen, FCCI is pleased to welcome you to this Monday afternoon presentation from the Inspired to Lead Conference at the Ritz -Carlton Dove Mountain Resort in Tucson, Arizona. This afternoon's keynote speaker is the founder and managing partner of a growing early stage venture fund in Chicago, Illinois. With a strong desire to invest in founder -focused, redemptive purposes, our speaker has established an investment strategy that empowers founders, businesses, and ultimately cultures to reflect the profound and enduring truths of our faith. Speaking from his desire to motivate greater levels of commitment to leadership and family well -being, would you please join in welcoming to the Ritz -Carlton Ballroom stage a compelling voice for healthy founders building healthy companies? Mark Phillips.

[SPEAKER_00]
Wow, that was an awesome video. Ken told me that it was going to be good, but that was fantastic. It's such a pleasure to be here. Thank you for having me. The timing of this is perfect because I want to start our conversation talking about food, actually. Let me take you back to the year 1938. The world was blissfully unaware of the culinary marvel that was about to be born out of what can only be described as a failed kitchen experiment. A talented young chef named Ruth Wakefield was whipping up a batch of chocolate cookies in her Toll House Inn in Massachusetts. Ruth ran into a bit of a snack. She ran out of baker's chocolate, and so she improvised, right? She took little chunks of semi -sweet chocolate, mixed it into the dough, and expected it to melt through. Well, Ruth was shocked when she realized that the chocolate chips didn't just melt through, they stayed put, giving birth to what is now an iconic treat, which is the chocolate chip cookie. Right? Amazing. It's just fantastic what can happen when we frame failure with the proper perspective, right? Maybe for the more practical folks in the audience, let's talk about the Post -it note. The year was 1968, and a talented young scientist named Spencer Silver at 3M was setting out to build a really ultra -strong adhesive. Well, Spencer didn't do all that well and came out with a particularly weak one. He thought it was a failure, right? At first glance, this thing wasn't going to work, but it was actually his colleague, Art Fry, who had a different idea. It was Art's aha moment while singing in church choir, mind you, where he realized that maybe we could use this weak adhesive in a really interesting way. So they decided to create the sticky note, right? The Post -it note, and use it as a reusable bookmark. Its ability to stick to the surface, be removed without leaving any residue. It was an innovation that's fundamentally changed the way we take notes, track our lives, and of course, for the business owners in the room, document strategic innovation meetings every single year. Right? Incredible. And if you're not convinced, let's go to one more industry. Let's talk about healthcare. The year is 1928. We're all the way back in, you know, the roaring 20s, and ultimately, there are infectious diseases roaming the world with very, very few cures in sight. There was a Scottish bacteriologist named Alexander Fleming. He was laboring tirelessly to find a solution, and weary and likely overworked, he left a petri dish of bacteria uncovered for the night. He came back expecting this to be an abject failure. The experiment he was working on wasn't going to work, but what he found was fascinating. Unknowingly, the, excuse me, the unknowingly, there was a mold called penicillium that had infiltrated the bacteria and killed the surrounding bacteria, opening the door to the world's first antibiotic, penicillin. Crazy, right? This chance encounter with mold, born out of what some might have considered a total failure, marked the beginning of a medical revolution, saving countless lives, and shaping the future of healthcare as we know it. So, as the amazing video told you, my name is Mark Phillips. I'm the founder and managing partner of 11 Tribes Ventures. We are an early stage venture fund based out of Chicago that was actually born out of my own personal failure. We'll get into that story in a little bit, but I started a healthcare company called Diasense while going through business school. And as I'll get into, we had to shut the business down. I was recently asked, what's the single most important experience of your life outside of faith and family, right? Those two things kind of take the cake. But what happened in your professional life that's really shaped the way that you perceive the world? For me, the answer to that question at first glance was, well, I started a company. I learned so much about managing a business and managing people and bringing my faith into intersection with my work. But as I reflected on the question, what I realized was shutting a company down was so much more impactful to my life. It taught me so much more about myself, taught me so much more about my relationship with God. And what I'm here to talk to you today about is really that idea of failure. I think this word failure gets a bad rap in our society, right? But ultimately, we have some questions that we can ask, right? Is failure fatal? What can we learn from it? What does God have to tell us about what failure does for our personal and professional and faith lives? And ultimately, I hope to show you that in order to understand God's full vision for our personal and professional lives, we must first experience a sense of emotional and spiritual poverty. We must experience failure. And I've used this phrase, really take a downward journey. So to frame the conversation, I want to start with the story from the Bible. Great place to start, right? And it's a story that maybe you haven't heard applied to the world of business before. It's the story of Joseph. We all know the basic tenets, right? Joseph is the most favored son. His brothers stage his death and sell him into slavery. He's manipulated and imprisoned while a slave in Potiphar's home. And ultimately, while in prison, he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and his baker. But there's some aspects of this story that I think are a little bit more underappreciated, shall we say. Let's start with the first that I think Joseph may have been a fairly intolerable little brother. Let's think about this, right? He walks around with fancy new clothes that his dad gave him. He tells his brothers that he's going to rule over them one day. If anyone has siblings, I'm the littlest brother of four brothers. If anyone has siblings, you know that is not a recipe for success. This shows me that Joseph hadn't been humbled yet. He had a vision. Yes, God gave him a vision. This is the really critical point here. He had a vision that God had given him to rule over his brothers. But that vision was so entirely far away from what God actually had in store. So yes, we're given visions, but we have to take this downward journey to fully understand and appreciate what God has in store for us. Second point, he remained obedient. Critical. Critical. Critical. God doesn't call us to success. He calls us to obedience. And let's look at the points where Joseph remained obedient. Well, he remained obedient against temptation while in Potiphar's home. He remained obedient in the depths of the prison when he probably thought his life was over. He could have said, I've got these skills God has given me. I can interpret dreams. But what's the point? What's the point? I'm just going to give up. And so that brings me to the third point, which is definitely the most important. Joseph gave God the glory. Joseph gave God the glory. Let's look at a verse from Genesis 41 to kind of unpack this. So Pharaoh, this, okay, so he's interpreted the dreams for cupbearer and baker. Pharaoh heard about it and he's calling Joseph up out of prison. Genesis 41, 14 says, So Pharaoh sent for Joseph and he was quickly brought from the dungeon. When he had shaved and changed his clothes, he came before Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to him, I had a dream and no one can interpret it. But I've heard it said of you that when you hear a dream, you can interpret it. Here's the most important verse. I cannot do it, Joseph replied to Pharaoh. But God will give Pharaoh the answer he desires. What a crazy verse. Let's put this into context, right? Think of the most powerful person in the world and then multiply that times 100. That's Pharaoh. One word out of his mouth and everything changes in Joseph's life. Joseph, I can promise you that if the president of United States comes up to me and says, Mark, you've got a special skill. Can you do it? The first words out of my mouth would be like, no, I'm sorry. I can't. So sorry. It would be, sure, let me deliver. But Joseph was humbled. He had taken the downward journey. And what he had realized was it wasn't about him. It was about God. And so I'd like to reframe verse 16 and use it as a framework for the rest of our conversation. Joseph's response is, can you interpret James? He says, no, I can't. But I serve the one who can. That's what he's saying here. And I think that's what a true humbling experience will do for us. So from here, I want to take you for three stories. Three stories from the marketplace that have occurred over the last handful of years that I think will hopefully illuminate the idea of what does this downward journey look like? And how does it ultimately bring to light God's true vision for our personal and professional careers? The first story is actually incredibly personal to me because it's about my dad. My father's name is Rich Phillips. He served for 35 years as a corporate attorney working for a small little company called Accenture, if anybody knows it. He was with them in the late 90s when they were Anderson Consulting and so helped navigate them through the Arthur Anderson and the Enron scandal, which is a whole story in and of itself. But ultimately, my dad spent his whole majority of his career with Accenture. He was given an opportunity, actually, towards the later half of his career to pursue the general counsel position of the company. And if you know anything about big corporate structures and general counsel positions, what my dad understood was that role, it really would put into conflict for him his priorities. What do I mean by that? I mean, his priorities were, number one, to be a present husband and father. Well, let me flip that. Number one, to be a child of God. Number two, to be a present husband and father. I was still a sophomore in high school when my dad was offered the opportunity. so here's the punchline. He turned it down. He turned down the general counsel position of Accenture. But here's the thing. God honored it. And to me, that rejection, that decision my dad made to take the path less traveled, if you will, that was his downward journey. Well, about three years after that decision was made, my dad was approached by the CEO of Accenture, a gentleman named Pierre Nanturn. And Pierre said, Rich, I need you to rewrite the conduct policy for Accenture. We haven't rewritten it in about 30 years. It needs an overhaul. Would you do it? My dad graciously and humbly accepted the role. And wouldn't you know it, the next Sunday at church, we're sitting there, I'm sitting right next to him, and the sermon series that was being started that week was a book on Proverbs and the everlasting and enduring nature of the wisdom of Proverbs. My dad had the inspiration that he needed. He spent six months pouring over the book of Proverbs, pulling out the salient wisdom that he felt like was good for not just our personal lives, but our professional and our business lives as well. Things like, kind words bring life, but cruel words crush, Proverbs 15.4. Or lazy hands make for poverty, and diligent hands bring wealth. My dad created a new conduct policy within Accenture, and he presented the new policy along with a specific action plan that tied global managing partner compensation to the adherence of the conduct policy. So let's put this into context, what's happening right now. These super powerful Accenture executives are being tied to biblical wisdom in the form of Proverbs. My dad didn't call it biblical. He didn't call it Christian. He called it conduct counts. He said, these are enduring truths that we know to be good, and this is how we should operate our business. He presented it to the board of directors of Accenture, and wouldn't you know it, it was unanimously ratified. I took a screenshot. I wish you could see it a little bit more closely, but on your phones, if you want to go to Accenture Code of Business Ethics, you'll pull up, make your conduct count. This was my father's work, and I'm incredibly proud of him, and I think he would tell you if he was up here, this was the most important thing he did from a professional perspective. But let me tie it back to our conversation today. Traditional advice would have been to take the opportunity to gain influence, become general counsel, and pursue a bigger role, but my dad chose a different path. He chose to be obedient to what he knew were his key priorities, and ultimately God honored that in an incredible way. The second story is that of an organization called Kehi Food Distributors. It's a local firm, actually, in Chicago. It's one of the largest food distributors in the world. I had the pleasure of meeting a gentleman named Rusty Bland, who's a 20 -year executive there, and now the executive director of the Kehi Cares Foundation. Rusty started at the firm in the early 2000s, and he had a vision while he was there for, man, what would it look like if we built a kingdom -based culture within our company that when people came to work, no matter their faith affiliations, they would leave with more in the tank than when they had arrived? I think this is a beautiful question, and one that we as believers can bring to the marketplace in so many different ways. Well, Rusty struggled with this for years. Year over year, would come up with new ideas how to build this culture, how to bring it to life, until in 2010, he took a trip with a few select colleagues to Honduras. They were headed there to help build the trees for impoverished communities, but as Rusty leaned into that experience, he found a vision for this kingdom -based culture. He was going to Honduras to heal, but ultimately he was the one being healed. And as he was going to serve, he was the one being served. In our culture, our Western American thinking is success is always framed as up and to the right, but upwardly mobile is a sentiment. But let's go back to the teachings of Jesus, right? What has Jesus taught us? He said things like, if you want to find your life, you must lose it first. He taught about how seeds don't really become what they're fully intended to be until they fall to the ground and die, and then they can multiply. That is the downward journey, isn't it? As business leaders, we must do the same. And while it is counterintuitive to culture, when we empty ourselves too, and we take this downward journey, we find our lives and experience the fullest life and the fullest business possible. Today, Rusty learned that in Honduras and brought this simple insight back to his company. All 400 senior executive level folks at Kehi take a trip to Honduras or elsewhere to perform some sort of mission trip every single year. That's regardless of their faith affiliations. That has ultimately led to a business culture that is built upon servant leadership and creates real value for each and every one of their employees. I don't think it's any accident that Kehi has since become the second largest food distributor in the world and recently surpassed a billion dollars in revenue. It's amazing. One more story for you from the marketplace, and then we'll watch a brief video. I'm honored to know a man named Pete Oaks. I wonder, I actually buy a show of hands. Does anyone else here know Pete Oaks? Can we get, yeah, I see a few hands out there. Incredible man, lives in Kansas. If you ever get the chance to meet him, I highly encourage it. He's one of the most God -honoring business leaders I've ever met. I called him in anticipation of this conversation with all of you, and I said, Pete, what was that downward journey like for you? When did you know that you had to humble yourself to become successful? And for those of you that know him, Pete didn't skip a beat, and in his low, powerful voice, Pete said, Mark, I was 41 years old. I was in the middle of a bad business deal, and I was about to go completely broke. I'd bought a bank, a failing bank at that, and we were being sued. And in my great wisdom, I decided to countersue, and I was burning $8,000 a day in legal fees. It's crazy. Desperate for resolution, desperate for a way out, Pete felt the Lord telling him to humble himself, empty his pride, to take the downward journey. Humbled and broken, Pete walked into the office of the man that was suing him. He dropped to his knees. This is a big man. Dropped to his knees and said, begged for forgiveness, begged for resolution. And here's the craziest part. As he looked up, he saw that the man had begun to weep. He was so overcome with emotion. He looked down at Pete and said, just one month prior, that he'd accepted Jesus Christ into his heart as his Lord and Savior. He was so frustrated with the mess that this lawsuit had created, that all he'd been asking God for was a way out. A way to end the debate. To end the lawsuit. The two men sat down. They agreed on terms. And to the chagrin of their legal teams, of course, they ended the lawsuit. At the age of 41, for the first time in his life, Pete realized that, as he says it, God's word makes good sense. God will get you to this emptied out place. But it's either going to be voluntarily or involuntarily. It's up to us to choose how. Pete has since gone on to form a company called Capital Three, which is focused on impact investing. And I'd like to play a brief video that really, it brings something to light, which I'll touch on after the video. But when we take this downward journey, what it allows us to do is to take the pressure off of ourselves and to co -create with our creator. I think Pete has done that in an exceptional and a beautiful way. And as he's building a business in a maximum security prison, which you'll hear about in just 10 seconds, I think Pete has brought incredible impact to the marketplace in a way that very few have. So let's play the video.

And so that's the connection I want to make here today is, and I'll actually go to a slide to get there, right? I think that downward journey, it does three things. It gives us the humility to admit we don't have all the answers. That's a dangerous person who doesn't need to be right in an organization. That's a dangerous person who doesn't have to have all the answers. And I don't think we get there until we accept that, no, it's not me, but I serve the one who does. Right? It gives us a resilient mentality, knowing that failure is not fatal. Resilience is a, I'll talk about it in a moment, but resilience is something I focus on all the time. Right? And I think the most resilient thing we can understand is that I don't have all the answers and it doesn't have to be me. And then the last is, and you heard Pete speak about it, it's a renewed energy for the opportunity to co -create with our creator. There's one last story that I'd like to share and it is my own. I launched this talk with a little bit of context into where I've come from. I started my career in consulting, management consulting. I went to business school at the University of Chicago. And while I was there, well, actually about six months prior to enrolling, my four -year -old nephew had been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. I knew very little about the situation. I didn't know what that marketplace looked like. He had gone into a coma. It was a pretty scary incident. And as his parents grappled with that disease and tried to figure out how to bring technology into the health outcomes of their little boy, I wanted to help solve that problem for them. So I started a company called Diasense. It was an IoT hardware device about yay big. It would help type 1 diabetics better measure their blood sugar, their insulin usage. It had a software platform built into it. It was a cool company. I took it through business school. We were doing great. We were going to pitch competitions and we were winning. I had a moment, I remember it pretty clearly, where I thought to myself, this is it. This is the thing I'm going to do for the next 10 years of my life. Well, I think God has a way of humbling us. I was on the involuntary side. Let's just go with that. I got to the end of my second year at business school. We had a seed round pulled together. We were going to raise capital to scale the business. And about four days before I'm supposed to close the round and take the capital, a billion dollar health tech incumbent based in Chicago released an identical product. And you can't make these things up, right? We had no intellectual property. We had filed conditional patents, but it didn't protect us. I called all the investors and 48 hours before I'm supposed to close this round and go right off into the sunset of the future of my life, all the investors back out and we ran out of cash. And so I share that story, right? Because I think that failure is so critical to my own personal journey. The next six months were pretty painful. I started working with coaches. I sought out mentors. I had to come to terms with the fact that I had attached my identity and my sense of self -worth as a Christ follower to the performance of diacence. And I'm here today to tell you that is a problem and that will lead to so much pain. I look back on it now and again, I was asked, what's the single most important experience of your life? That failure behind meeting Jesus Christ and meeting my wife, that failure is the single most important experience of my life. And I think it is the single greatest gift God has ever given me. It showed me that my identity is not in my company. It showed me that my self -worth is tied to my relationship with Jesus and not the thing that I can build. And so I shut diacence down. I became very passionate about the topic of failure, obviously, but I wanted to do something about it. And to use the Joseph story, I felt God give me a vision to think about how do we support entrepreneurs? I think in the world of business and for my purposes, startups, we've got two connected but not correlated outcomes. The business outcome is what, as a society, we are trained to measure. Exit valuations and cash flow and IRR, all the things, right? But the other side of the equation is just as important. But we don't talk about it as often. We've coined it the founder outcome, the CEO outcome, whatever phrase you want to use. As a startup investor, we focus on founders. And what I believe is that traditional venture capital and traditional capitalism is focused on a maximization function. It wants to maximize for financial outcomes. But true capitalism, and as you heard Pete say, it's not just about the financial, it's an optimization function. How do we optimize for business? Excuse me. How do we optimize for financial, for human, for social, and for environmental capital? That's what we're focused on. so at 11 Tribes, we exist not just to build for business outcomes, but we invest to optimize for both founder and business outcomes. How do we do that? Well, a couple of different ways. We allocate 2 % of every invested dollar directly to the entrepreneurs we work with for them to put towards their own entrepreneurial resilience. We talked about ILI, training and equipping leaders to have an impact in the marketplace. We can't expect them to go out and be successful right off the bat. They need training. They need to be equipped. So that work of ILI and so many other leadership development agencies across the country is just incredible. We also bring around the entrepreneurs we work with, subject matter experts who also understand that, man, life isn't just about having successful financial outcomes. It's about building in a way that's sustainable and in a way that makes life worth living to keep it very simple. And so that's what we're doing at 11 Tribes Ventures. I am so passionate about failure and the idea that we don't have to have all the answers. How do we co -create with our creator? These are the things that I really want us to be thinking about. And so as I close my remarks, there's a few questions that I would ask, right? If we can't trust God in our own disappointment, how can we expect to trust him with fulfilled dreams? If we can't trust him with betrayal, how can we trust him with lifelong relationships? And if we can't trust him with failure, how can we expect to trust him in success? Good afternoon. My name is John Chapman. I'm the Chief Executive Officer and the Chief Investment Strategist for Clearwater Capital Partners. It is my great privilege to welcome you here this afternoon to the beautiful Medina Country Club. So glad to see so many familiar faces and quite a few new ones as well. Clearwater Capital was formed nearly 20 years ago, founded by me and my friend Al Krause, who is now our CFO. And what a journey it's been. This summer marks my 43rd year on Wall Street. And I can tell you with great confidence the last 20 have been by far the best. I have the privilege of leading a very talented and very dedicated team of professionals. And we have an excellent program for you here today. A lot of our clients are entrepreneurs. They have businesses. They have assets of all different types across a wide range of asset classes. Today we'll be talking about exit strategies and what business owners may want to be thinking about as it relates to that. I do warn you ahead of time, we set out to pack as much insight into the next two hours as possible. And it's going to get pretty intense. And if two hours from now you're feeling a little exhausted, you'll see our team in the back high -fiving one another because that means that we did our job. But remember, this is just the beginning, really, of a conversation. We want to set into motion some critical thinking, some questions, a curiosity around the possibilities for those business owners who may be thinking about monetization and what that means, both within families and perhaps even with third -party private equity and all sorts of different things. I think culture can be a big component of it as well, and we could talk about that for another 20 minutes, I'm sure. As one client family says, it's just expensive to grow up. And so all of these areas of work and the intentionality that needs to be brought there, if there's one thought from today, really it is that planning aspect and getting out in front of it.

documents.text:
[SPEAKER_01]
This is the Investor Connect podcast program. I'm Hal T. Martin. I'm the host of the show in which we interview angel investors, venture capital, family offices, private equity, and many other investors for early stage and growth companies. I hope you enjoy this episode. Investor Connect is a 501c3 nonprofit dedicated to the education of investors and startups for fundraising. Please consider donating $100 to the program to help others in their investor and entrepreneur journey. You can find the donate button on the InvestorConnect.org website. Well, hello. This is Hal Marchant with Investor Connect. Today, I'm here with Christina Chappell, director of 11 Tribe Ventures. 11 Tribes Ventures is an early stage venture fund that proactively invests in the well -being of entrepreneurs. The company provides innovative, founder -focused venture capital investment to early stage technology companies in non -traditional technology hubs across the country. Christina, thank you for joining us.

[SPEAKER_00]
Paul, it is so great to be here. Thank you for having me.

[SPEAKER_01]
So tell us more about your background before joining 11 Tribe Ventures.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yes. So 11 Tribes is based in Chicago, and I drove up here six months ago from the South without a friend or family member in sight because I was so compelled by the thesis of what we're building here. I have a background in city planning and entrepreneurship. Back home in Atlanta, I launched two community engagement initiatives, one at my school and one in the greater Atlanta community, which both scaled up and brought me to UNC Chapel Hill on scholarship with a program called Moorhead Cain, which punted me into a number of different environments, giving me experience in teaching and consulting. One of my summer internships, I ended up at a private equity firm, and that was my first experience into the world of finance and loved that, but wanted to move earlier stage. And so I've found 11 Tribes. I really appreciated our thesis and really how we were able to integrate our values with our work. And that's what made me decide to move to Chicago to join full -time as employee number one to the managing partner, Mark Phillips.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. So what excites you right now?

[None]
You

[SPEAKER_00]
know, something that I found very exciting, Paul, is just the rise of remote and hybrid work. We're finding entrepreneurs who are tucked away in what we call competitive geographies. So non -traditional tech hubs, so not San Francisco or New York, more like Chattanooga and Cincinnati and Indianapolis who are building great businesses. And also given just our current macroeconomic environment here in February of 2023, we're seeing tons of big tech layups. So I think that some great companies are going to be formed in these days. And I'm also just personally excited to be placed here in Chicago. There are several funds here who are working to activate more early stage capital and more LPs from the women and wealthy individuals in the area who have not had exposure to venture capital as an asset class before. So I'm excited to be investing in this time.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. Great. Well, you see a lot of startups and a lot of investors out there. What's your advice for people investing in early stage venture funds? What do you tell them to do before they write that check?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yes. For LPs, I think the first, and it's top of mind, is just finding a firm that you are aligned with from a values perspective. And if you're able to find a team deploying capital in a way that you think are advancing good outside of just financial returns, I think that that is really special, especially if you are running checks into early stage funds, possibly for the first time. And I also would give advice of finding teams who will be transparent with you. I know here at 11 Tribes, we are committed to full transparency with our LPs. And so what that looks like is we have quarterly LP reports and quarterly calls with our LPs to give them status updates on each of the companies in our portfolio and sort of where our fund is presently and where we're going.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. So what's your advice for people running venture funds? What do you tell them to do before they launch that new fund?

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, you know what they say, venture is fully a relationships business. So I think it's important to just get your boots on the ground, especially in those underfinanced geographies, as we see more and more people spread out from MSF in New York and Boston. And so if people are able to establish relationships with operators in those areas or other early stage investors, seeing that's how you're going to get access to the best deals and ultimately add the most value to founders as well. So the other piece of advice I would give is founders are looking for more than just financial capital these days. So as an emerging fund, we have to be really clear of what's our value add and our niche alongside of the check that we're writing and how can we get access to the best cap tables and the best co -investors.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. Well, tell us more about that. How do you see the industry evolving from here with that in mind?

[SPEAKER_00]
I mean, I think one of the large things I'm seeing is just who are the players in the industry? And I, in Chicago, at least, I'm seeing more and more access to that. So who are we investing in? I mean, our founders look different. And for 11 tribes, 38 % of our portfolio from Fund One has a female in the founding team. And 40 % of our Fund One portfolio are also from minority backgrounds. And so who is getting the checks written? And then who are the LPs in these funds? I think that I'm seeing evolution there. And I mean, for Fund Two at 11 Tribes, we're doing a parallel fund structure that allows more people to participate by giving flexibility on minimums too. So we're seeing more and more creative ways for funds to establish themselves and engage more people who've maybe not had exposure to the asset class before.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. And what do think is the biggest change we're going to see in the VC fund world in the next few years?

[SPEAKER_00]
I think what we have seen is that there's more and more competition with just the number of emerging funds and smaller players raising first -time funds or second funds. And I think that raises the bar and elevates the industry as a whole. So that's something that's very exciting to me. And I also think that that is actually breeding more collaboration in the industry. I know we have gotten sharper on who do we want to invest alongside. And that's going to, what we believe, increase the pie for everyone and venture as a whole too.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. Well, so let's talk about your investment thesis. What exactly is it and how did you arrive at it?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, we do take a thesis -driven approach here at 11 Tribes. And we have three main components to that, one of which I've spoken to, which is we target competitive geographies. And so we are a Midwest -based fund. We lean into that. And we have a strong Midwest presence in our Fund One portfolio. But we also are looking for the best builders in Atlanta, Georgia, in Columbia, South Carolina, in Texas. And so that's one angle. The next is that we are a seed stage fund. So we are some of the first checks in, typically following on with a lead investor to close that round. And the other piece that really sets us apart and the reason why I came to join the firm is just the amount of support that we assemble around our founding teams. Every check that we write, we have made a commitment to invest 2 % on top of that check directly to the founding teams for them to invest in their well -being and development. And so usually that looks like we're writing $250K to $300K checks, which means those founders are getting $5,000 to $6,000 in a bank account for them to use either on an executive coach geared specifically for founders or for a therapist. I think, I know my managing partner, Mark, has sat across the table from countless founders who have said, if only you were here five years ago when I was raising my round, then maybe I would still be married or I would still have a relationship with my children. And so we think we want to help our founders build great businesses that have the potential to affect cultures and change, but not at the expense of the things that are most important in their lives. And the other piece of what we surround our founding teams with is what we call our venture partner platform. And so we have identified industry experts and really operators who have started and exited companies scattered all around the country. I mean, most of our venture partners are located in these competitive geographies. And they come on to be a mentor and coach to that founder, getting in the trench with them. And we compensate them with GP Carey here at 11 Tribes. So we are trying to rethink the traditional business model of venture and how we allocate resources to allocate more around our founders that will increase the pie for all people touching.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. Well, what startups in your portfolio are you most excited about?

[None]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]
me know. Two come to mind, Hal. The first is a Chicago -based company called KeyWise AI, and they are a consumer healthcare company. We say KeyWise is a bit for your brain, basically. Through a five -year NIH -funded grant, the KeyWise team built an AI platform that tracks brain function objectively and precisely. So the KeyWise system uses keystrokes on your smartphone to measure things like processing speed, attention, impulse control, and mood stability. And their patent -protected system is currently live on the App Store. I'd encourage everyone to go download it and give it a try. The team is focused on its B2B2C growth strategy in 23. They're targeting hospital systems, clinics, and outpatient entities that will use the platform to help track patient health and adherence post -hospitalization. And the other company in our portfolio that we are really excited about is a Cincinnati -based company called GetTogether. They play in the future of workspace. And GetTogether is building the fastest, easiest way to schedule meetings by embedding AI directly into any messaging platform. So think text, Slack, Teams, and even email. And fundamentally, GetTogether believes that any human connection today starts with a message, and they want to be the platform that makes connecting frictionless. They just received follow -on capital from Drive Capital, which is one of the largest funds in the Midwest. And they just closed a patent application for their cross -channel chat AI scheduling feature, making GetTogether the only centralized scheduling AI that can be used across multiple communication channels. So we're very excited for both of those teams.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, sound like great startups. Congratulations on those. So what do you think are the main challenges early -stage venture funds face today?

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, venture is an industry where there can be a lot of hype and a lot of noise. And so I think for funds who maybe have less access to good deal flow, it can be difficult to remain disciplined and cut through that noise. I mean, we see ChatGPT being on every news article today. And any startup that is now touching AI or generative AI, it's easy for those valuations to become inflated. Here at 11Tribes, we really do remain disciplined. Our average valuation cap in our Fund One portfolio is just under $8 million. We made the bulk of our investments in 2021 and early 2022. So that was a time when valuations were very inflated and we were able to stay anchored. So I think that that is a challenge for an early -stage fund. And then also just making sure that you have a comprehensive due diligence process. I know here we have quite a hefty process. I run point on that. And we're not just going with even what our co -investors have to say, but we have a lot of framework on how we vet companies. And not even just the financial side or industry trends, but we also administer personality assessments to our founders with the Colby Index and StrengthsFinder to ensure that our founding teams are the best people to build and are equipped well with teammates with complementary skill sets that allow them to, what we say, ride a lion and live, which is basically what our founders are doing here.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, Well, you see a lot of new businesses and business models and technologies out there. If you could start a business tomorrow, what would that business be?

[SPEAKER_00]
I love this question, Hall. You know, I toyed around with starting a Pokemon Go for intentional acts of kindness. I was going to call it the Love Challenge. And, you I think for my generation, Gen Z, it's easy to kind of live for these mountaintop moments in life and discount the beauty amidst our mundane daily rhythms. I think even with possibly a downside of remote work is just people are not being as neighborly or tethered in communities. And so I think if we are able to shift our perspective and build habits to be on the lookout for other people and make small differences or build a small amount of margin into our day to more meaningfully connect with the people around us, that that will have a massive impact on communities as a whole and our own lives as individuals.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, great. Well, in the last few minutes that we have here today, what should we cover that we haven't?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, language that we use here at 11 Tribes is we want to help our founders build without burnout. And I know for entrepreneurs particularly, I mean, this is a population of people who really deal with mental health issues. So I think making sure that you are a healthy founder, which will then hopefully lead to a healthy company and healthy employees and healthy returns for LPs. It's just really important to not compromise on those most important things in life by being head down, trying to make something from nothing. So, and then also I think it's important to note that venture as an asset class performed particularly well in recessions. I know Cambridge Associates has some really strong data out there that I'd encourage everybody listening to this podcast to go and check out. But even for a median venture fund, median performance is 2.4x. So you're doubling your money. then some, you know, 11 Trumps were setting out to be a top decile fund. So hopefully we are returning much more than 2.4. But I think typically people see venture as this boom or bust area, when in reality those numbers actually are quite different. So doing research is key.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. So how best for listeners to get back in touch with you?

[SPEAKER_00]
Listeners can find me on LinkedIn and find the Lev and Shrouds on LinkedIn and Twitter. It's the best way.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. We'll put that in the show notes. I want to thank you for joining us today and hope to have you back for a follow -up soon.

[None]
Thanks

[SPEAKER_00]
all. Pleasure to be here.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank Investor Connect helps investors interested in startup funding. In this podcast series, experienced investors share their experience and advice. You can learn more at InvestorConnect.org. Halty Martin is the director of Investor Connect, which is a 501c3 nonprofit dedicated to the education of investors for early -stage funding. All opinions expressed by Hal and podcast guests are solely their own opinions and do not reflect the opinion of Investor Connect. This podcast is for informational purposes only and should not be relied upon as a basis for investment decisions. Investor Connect.

[SPEAKER_00]
Welcome to the Masters of Resilience podcast. This show is an exploration of the unseen and unheard stories of adversity that shape the journeys of high performers. These conversations will help you better understand the mindset, habits, and behaviors that empower these exceptional leaders to endure the most challenging moments of their careers and emerge stronger than ever. Your hosts are Ryan Seeger and Mark Phillips. Let's dive in to more.

[SPEAKER_03]
Jeremy, thank you for joining us at the Masters of Resilience podcast. It's great to be here. We appreciate the time and excited to hear more about your story and the work you're doing through the field school. I think to just jump right in, I'd love it if you could share a story with our audience about a moment or an experience in your life where you really feel like resilience had a big role to play in what you were able to accomplish.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah, I think just diving into the field school story. So just to give people some context, this was nine years ago that my wife and I led a team of people to start a intentionally diverse classical Christian school on the west side of Chicago. So the idea was, let's create a world -class school that's designed for children from low -income families. And that was just a, I mean, great idea. But like, how do you actually do that? And nine years later, I can just point to, I don't know, maybe the kind of year zero, year one, year five. Now, like learning to endure a long time in something hard. This decision that we made to start the school has like changed my career trajectory. It affected our finances as a family significantly. It forced me to grow as a leader. You know, there's a lot of different stakeholders in a school. And now we have something like 60 employees. There's a lot of like faith required to do something like this or persistence. We are a very diverse school as well. And so learning to really work with people from different backgrounds, it has been an amazing privilege, but also a kind of trial and all sorts of differences. I think, but to kind of give one story, there was a time during COVID where we had a number of really intense personnel changes. We had the principal of the school kind of had to step down in an emergency setting. And I just remember really, really long nights, lots of different important communication points and just sort of feeling like very alone in that. And God provided what we needed. Amazing people stepped up to help. But it was one of those times where you're like, this is not one long night of work or one week. It's like month after month of really grueling trial and this belief that what you do matters

[None]
and the

[SPEAKER_02]
Lord sees it and you're not going to regret doing the right thing. But it was really, really hard. It was really, really hard. Some of that time.

And it was striking how much, like, we lived in the neighborhood not far from it. [None]

[SPEAKER_02]
should be something we are engaging in a systematic kind of profound way. So I moved to Chicago and started training special education teachers in Chicago. Deal Highlights - NQS (National Quality Systems)
Founded by multi-time entrepreneur Mark Feinberg, NQS is a vertical AI platform designed to streamline trauma registry management for hospital emergency departments. The company addresses a highly specialized domestic market of approximately 2,400 trauma registry departments—a space previously served by a single, broad-based incumbent whose undifferentiated software left users deeply underserved.
11 Tribes co-invested alongside lead investor Long Run Capital, committing an initial $750,000 check into a priced seed round at an $8 million post-money valuation, with the total raise of $2 million split between the two firms. A defining feature of the investment was NQS's 16 signed hospital contracts at the time of closing—despite the product being six to eight weeks from launch—a rare validation of both market urgency and founder credibility.
Operating partner Carolyn Wilson, former COO of the University of Chicago Health System, provided critical domain expertise during diligence. The round closed in March 2025, the product launched within weeks, and NQS has since grown rapidly. 11 Tribes has made two additional investment tranches, including a recent $750,000 follow-on that effectively constitutes a Series A.

Through The Valley
By Mark Phillips
Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.
New episodes every Wednesday.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.

The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yours
Why he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointment
What it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successor

The letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first time

Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom.
Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade.
Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years.

Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in.
He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had.
Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage.

Why Brutal Honesty Is the Kindest Thing an Investor Can Do, with VC Coach Charlie O’Donnell
For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped.
The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. Charlie ran Brooklyn Bridge Ventures as a solo first-check investor across more than 100 companies, and when he looked at the two available ways to keep doing it into his 40s (hire a younger version of himself, or stop looking at anything pre-revenue) he decided he'd rather not do the job at all than do it that way.
Mark Phillips sits with Charlie on what it costs to hold a career loosely: the ice cream shop that went to zero and the conversation he never had with those founders, the marathon he ran badly and blamed on the wind, the 80 days in the NICU where three term sheets got signed, and the firefighter father who played tennis in the morning and did tax returns in the afternoon and was content.

From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today.
In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth.
They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear.
Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers.

The podcast features a deep dive into the world of small business acquisitions, highlighting the significant opportunity presented by the ongoing transfer of ownership from retiring Baby Boomers.
What is acquisition entrepreneurship? It is the practice of searching for and buying established, profitable small businesses - usually from a retiring owner. Fruition Capital invests in these businesses.
I invited Jason Ehrlich, Managing Partner of Fruition Capital on ATLalts to discuss why he believes investing in the acquisition of small businesses can allow investors to take advantage of what he believes are four key factors:
Generational transfer of US small businesses owned by Baby Boomers is underway. Greater then 3 million profitable businesses owned by 65+ year-old owners will change hands in the next 5-10 yearsAttractive acquisition prices of 3x-5x avg. acquisition multiples (of EBITDA) for target businesses.Probability of failure is low as only 2.1% of SBA 7a Business Acquisition Loans defaulted in 2023The Chance of attractive performance is high as 75% of sesarch entrepreneur investors achieved an IRR of 20% according to one study.
Jason Ehrlich, Managing Partner of Fruition Capital, discusses how his firm focuses on investing in B2B companies with stable earnings and a repeat customer base, which he refers to as "enduring profitability." The conversation emphasizes the attractive valuations available in this space, often at 3x-5x multiples of EBITDA, and the low failure rates associated with these businesses, particularly in the context of SBA 7a loans. Ehrlich also elaborates on the unique structure of Fruition Capital, which differentiates itself by partnering closely with entrepreneurs while providing significant capital and operational support. As the episode unfolds, listeners gain insights into the strategies and criteria that make Fruition Capital a leader in this niche market, ultimately aiming to preserve and grow local businesses in communities across the U.S.
The impending retirement of Baby Boomer small business owners creates a unique landscape for investment, one that Fruition Capital is keen to navigate. The podcast sheds light on the economic opportunities that arise from the generational shift in business ownership, particularly in light of the favorable valuations available—typically three to five times EBITDA for these enterprises. With a low default rate of approximately 2.1% on SBA 7(a) loans, the primary financing method for such acquisitions, investors are presented with a compelling case for entering this market.
Ehrlich elaborates on Fruition Capital's stringent investment criteria, underscoring the firm’s commitment to stability and enduring profitability. By intentionally avoiding tech-heavy or cyclically volatile industries, Fruition ensures that its investments are grounded in businesses that have demonstrated resilience over time. The conversation also touches on the structural elements of deals, such as seller notes and equity rollovers, which serve to align the interests of the sellers and the new owners, thus facilitating a seamless transition of leadership while preserving the legacy of these local businesses. This model not only safeguards the interests of investors but also places the entrepreneurs in a position to succeed as they take the reins of these established firms.
Furthermore, the episode highlights the broader societal impact of Fruition Capital's investment strategy. By empowering a new generation of entrepreneurs to take over small businesses, Fruition aims to keep jobs within local communities and foster economic stability. Clients can buy and sell 100+ digital assets with deep liquidity and low slippage through Abra including both crypto/fiat and crypto/crypto pairs
Earn Yield
Abra offers a variable yield on BTC, ETH, SOL and stablecoins through separately managed accounts (SMAs).

Clients can borrow against their digital asset collateral to unlock liquidity.
Customized Investment Strategies
For more sophisticated clients, Abra can create customized delta-neutral portfolio strategies combining DeFi trading, lending and market-making.
Abra’s RIA operates a separately managed account model, this is crucial for transparency and security, as clients are not liabilities on Abra’s balance sheet, and they retain title to their assets (i.e. they are never commingled – which has been a historic issue in crypto).
Before Abra, Marissa founded Quantum Global Management, an investment firm focused on thematic investment in the building blocks of Web 3 and lending and DeFi strategies in digital assets and cofounded Ark Advisors, an advisory and investment firm focused on the digital asset space.

Mike highlights the significance of eligibility criteria and concentration limits. documents.text:
Through The Valley - Podcast - Apple Podcasts
Through The Valley
Mark Phillips
0.0 (0)
Emprendimiento
Cada semana
Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.
New episodes every Wednesday.
Episodio más reciente
Del más reciente al más antiguo
Del más antiguo al más reciente
Episodios
hace 4 días
Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout. What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die. Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born. In this episode: • What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair • The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working • Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness • The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time • How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today • Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it • What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com. EPISODE CHAPTERS 00:00 The valley 02:50 October 15, 2008 04:30 Two of his three biggest clients disappear 07:58 The offer he turned down 10:12 Three years, 20-hour days, a 1-in-10 shot 15:04 The letter 17:29 "Who here is a lonely entrepreneur?" 20:11 Why he says he never felt lonely 39:00 Why AI feels like 2008 again 50:57 The worst night in the valley
48 min
16 sep
Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement. He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now. Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him. In this episode: The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yoursWhy he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointmentWhat it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successorHow he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't saveThe letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first timeWhy he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exitThe Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news Subscribe for new episodes of Through the Valley every week. Watch on YouTube, listen on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Timestamps: 00:00 Intro 02:21 CoachUp was his identity 03:48 What the stress was doing to his body 06:59 When investor incentives stop matching yours 07:53 The middle range, where founders get replaced 08:47 The board’s offer, and helping pick his successor 09:42 Why he said yes: the thirty people he hired 12:24 The napkin math on preferred stock 15:55 President and chairman, “which means nothing” 17:04 Every good idea undermining his own replacement 19:04 What boxing taught him about getting hit 20:02 Running through Boston to his mentor’s office 21:40 The letter, read out loud 25:24 Telling ten employees the money was gone 26:00 Out of money, and the flight to California 26:56 Buying back in, and the turnaround 33:20 Start it, join it, or buy it 35:17 Fall in love with the problem 41:27 Building Acquisition Lab 46:08 The injury that ended his playing career
50 min
9 sep
Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom. Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade. Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years. In this episode: - The 24 hours between finding it himself and hearing the number - Why telling his parents was harder than hearing the diagnosis - What three weeks of not knowing does to someone who built his life on competence - Jewelers Row, twenty cents on the dollar, and the moment Alloy became obvious - The customer who asked to speak to the founder and had them both crying on the phone - Learning to control the controllable, and the chapter he doesn’t get to read for five years - The letter from a friend of eighteen years, and what he’d tell himself on the worst night Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Brandon’s company, The Alloy Market, sends a free evaluation kit to anyone looking to sell gold. 48 min
1 sep
Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in. He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had. Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage. In this episode: • Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation • The Godfather scene he read a month before everything came apart, and why it stayed with him • What he actually said when a counselor asked the room about God • Playing a kids' board game in treatment and feeling his side hurt from laughing for the first time in years • What his father wrote about Justin's lowest moment, and where his relationship with him sits now • Why there is shame in getting sober and none in the harm that came before it • The alcohol-free movement he did not know existed until it was growing in front of him • What he would say if he could sit with himself on the worst night: take this in, and get to work Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. You can find The Maze at themazenyc.com, on Instagram at @themazenyc, and on LinkedIn. Timestamps: 00:00 Intro 02:32 January 2008, and what the end looked like 03:56 The sister who would not let it go 04:24 Never having known a sober person 05:13 The book he was reading when it turned 08:10 What happens without someone in your corner 09:07 Through the valley: how dark it got 09:48 Arriving at rehab on Super Bowl Sunday 11:10 Borrowing hope from a football team 12:23 Something insignificant that carried enormous weight 13:10 Faith as an evolving process, and what seeking means 15:16 Laughing until his side hurt for the first time in years 17:47 The moment with his brother 18:45 What his father wrote about that season 20:48 What the word shame actually means here 22:57 Shown the light in the strangest of places 25:06 Really being awake 36:13 How The Maze started with coffee 38:20 Still reeling from Covid, and what fake connection looks like 43:01 What he would say to himself on the worst night 45:13 Who The Maze is actually for
46 min
25 ago
Why Brutal Honesty Is the Kindest Thing an Investor Can Do, with VC Coach Charlie O’Donnell
For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped. The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. Charlie ran Brooklyn Bridge Ventures as a solo first-check investor across more than 100 companies, and when he looked at the two available ways to keep doing it into his 40s (hire a younger version of himself, or stop looking at anything pre-revenue) he decided he'd rather not do the job at all than do it that way. Mark Phillips sits with Charlie on what it costs to hold a career loosely: the ice cream shop that went to zero and the conversation he never had with those founders, the marathon he ran badly and blamed on the wind, the 80 days in the NICU where three term sheets got signed, and the firefighter father who played tennis in the morning and did tax returns in the afternoon and was content. In this episode: • Why Charlie stopped raising funds while the option to continue was still open • The tradeoff he now tells every founder about before they take a check • How to hold "good investor" as a job rather than an identity • What 16 collapsed triathletes reveal about experienced high performers • The rounded-up revenue number that quietly ends a fundraise • What his father's illness taught him about asking what a person actually needs • The one thing he realized far too late about being a partner at home Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Charlie's book, Founder Unfriendly: What Investors Won't Tell You About Getting Funded, is available wherever you buy books, and his newsletter has been running at thisisgoingtobebig.com since 2004.
52 min
18 ago
From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today. In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth. They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear. Investing in People, Not Unicorns - Mark Phillips - 11 Tribes
Impact Investing Roadshow
56m
Mark Phillips, Founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, joins Impact Investing Roadshow to discuss his firm's founder-first venture capital thesis and their investment in NQS (National Quality Systems), a vertical AI platform transforming trauma registry management for U.S. hospital emergency departments.
Get The Full Episode Notes Here
Mark Phillips
Founder, 11 Tribes Ventures
Email | LinkedIn | Website
Masters of Resilience Podcast | Co-hosted Mark Phillips and Ryan Seger
Deal Highlights - NQS (National Quality Systems)
Founded by multi-time entrepreneur Mark Feinberg, NQS is a vertical AI platform designed to streamline trauma registry management for hospital emergency departments. The company addresses a highly specialized domestic market of approximately 2,400 trauma registry departments—a space previously served by a single, broad-based incumbent whose undifferentiated software left users deeply underserved.
11 Tribes co-invested alongside lead investor Long Run Capital, committing an initial $750,000 check into a priced seed round at an $8 million post-money valuation, with the total raise of $2 million split between the two firms. A defining feature of the investment was NQS's 16 signed hospital contracts at the time of closing—despite the product being six to eight weeks from launch—a rare validation of both market urgency and founder credibility.
Operating partner Carolyn Wilson, former COO of the University of Chicago Health System, provided critical domain expertise during diligence. The round closed in March 2025, the product launched within weeks, and NQS has since grown rapidly. 11 Tribes has made two additional investment tranches, including a recent $750,000 follow-on that effectively constitutes a Series A.
I'd love to connect with you on LinkedIn. You can find me here.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley
Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.
Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com.

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.
In this episode:
The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yours
Why he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointment
What it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successor
How he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't save
The letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first time
Why he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exit
The Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news
